definition: Treatment given after the main treatment (usually surgery) to lower the risk of the cancer coming back.
Having fewer red blood cells than normal. This can make you feel tired, weak, or short of breath.
Not cancer. Benign tumors don't spread to other parts of the body.
A procedure where a small sample of tissue is removed and checked under a microscope to see if it is cancer.
Medicine that kills cancer cells. It can be given as a pill or through a vein (IV). Usually given in cycles with rest periods in between.
A research study where new treatments are tested with volunteers. Often a way to access new options before they're widely available.
A type of X-ray that takes detailed pictures of the inside of the body from different angles.
Feeling very tired — more than just being sleepy. Cancer-related fatigue is different from normal tiredness and doesn't always go away with rest.
Treatment that helps your own immune system fight cancer. Different from chemotherapy — works with your body instead of directly killing cells.
The body's response to injury or infection. Can cause redness, swelling, heat, or pain.
Cancerous. Malignant tumors can grow and spread to other parts of the body.
When cancer spreads from where it started to another part of the body.
A scan that uses magnets and radio waves (not X-rays) to make detailed pictures of the body. It's loud but painless.
Feeling like you might throw up. Common with chemotherapy. Many medications can help — tell your care team if it happens.
Numbness, tingling, or pain in your hands or feet. Can be a side effect of some chemotherapy drugs.
Having fewer white blood cells than normal, which makes it harder to fight infections. Often caused by chemotherapy.
A doctor who specializes in treating cancer.
Care that focuses on relieving symptoms and improving quality of life. It's NOT the same as hospice — you can get palliative care at any stage.
A detailed report from a pathologist describing what was found in a biopsy or surgery sample.
A scan that uses a small amount of radioactive sugar to show how active cells are. Cancer cells often show up because they use more energy.
The likely outcome or course of a disease. This is an estimate, not a guarantee — everyone's journey is different.
High-energy rays that kill cancer cells. Usually painless — you don't feel anything during the treatment itself.
When cancer comes back after treatment. Can happen months or years later.
When signs and symptoms of cancer are reduced or gone. Can be partial (some signs remain) or complete (no signs found).
An unwanted effect of treatment. Everyone reacts differently — some people have many, others have few.
How doctors describe how much cancer is in the body and whether it has spread. Usually stages 1-4.
Sores or inflammation in the mouth. Common with some chemotherapies. Talk to your care team about mouth rinses that can help.
Drugs that attack specific features of cancer cells. Different from chemotherapy — it's more precise.
Having fewer platelets than normal, which makes it easier to bruise or bleed.
An abnormal growth of cells. Can be benign (not cancer) or malignant (cancer).
A substance in blood or tissue that can be measured. Some cancers produce these — doctors use them to track how treatment is going.
A scan that uses sound waves to make pictures of the body. Painless — the same technology used in pregnancy scans.
The number of white blood cells in your blood. These cells fight infection. Low counts mean you need to be more careful about germs.
